name: Theory and construct development
definition: Turning a loose idea about behavior into a claim that data can test. That means defining each concept, saying how the concepts connect, and stating what result would count as evidence.
proof: I developed the theory behind a COVID-19 field study, a study of fans and their favorite characters, a review of smartphones and wellbeing, my thesis, and my dissertation.

name: Experimental design
definition: Planning a study so a difference between groups can be traced to one cause. Chance decides who gets which condition, everything else stays the same, and the outcome is measured the same way for everyone.
proof: I designed and ran six studies for my dissertation, with each plan registered in advance, and recruited more than 3,000 people. My master's thesis was a registered experiment with 305 participants.

name: Longitudinal and repeated-measures design
definition: Planning a study that measures the same people more than once, such as daily diaries or follow-ups. One person's answers are related to each other. The analysis has to account for that so it can separate change over time from differences between people.
proof: I ran a 15-day behavior-change study with 560 people recruited and 455 retained. I also managed seven-day student diary studies, with about four surveys a day.

name: Causal and quasi-experimental methods
definition: Estimating what a program or event changed when people cannot be assigned at random. Methods include difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity, and matching. Each compares a treated group with a similar group and rests on assumptions that must be stated.
proof: At CSUN Institutional Research I ran a regression discontinuity analysis at the 15-unit load cutoff, then matched comparison groups on student records. In my dissertation's randomized before-and-after study I tested the intervention-by-condition interaction, a difference-in-differences structure. Graduate courses trained me in instrumental variables.

name: Crossover trial analysis
definition: Analyzing a study in which each person gets every treatment in turn, so each person serves as their own comparison. The analysis has to account for the order, the time period, and effects that carry over from one treatment to the next.
also: Secondary analysis of a randomized trial
proof: I am first author on a 2026 paper analyzing a randomized, double-blind crossover trial of a ghrelin-receptor blocker in 29 people with alcohol use disorder. The NIH team designed the trial. I ran the analysis and made the figures.

name: Mixed-methods program evaluation
definition: Judging whether a program works by collecting, analyzing, and combining numbers and words. Surveys and outcome data show how much changed, and interviews and open comments show why. Joining the two gives a fuller answer than either alone.
proof: I evaluated a university summer-skills program with focus groups, surveys, and student outcome data. I presented the results at departmental meetings.

name: Research synthesis
definition: Pulling the findings of many studies together to answer one question. The question and the rules for including studies are set in advance, and every step is documented to limit bias.
proof: I co-wrote a published review of how smartphones affect wellbeing. I synthesized the evidence for a COVID-19 social-contact paper and pooled the raw data from eight experiments.

name: Open and reproducible research
definition: Working so others can check the results. That means writing the research plan down and registering it before collecting data, then sharing materials and code. Any analysis that was not in the plan is labeled as such.
proof: I write my analysis plan down and register it publicly before I look at results. I share code and materials, and I co-founded a campus open-science group.

name: Digital behavior and technology effects
definition: Studying how using phones, apps, games, and online platforms relates to what people think, feel, and do.
proof: I studied how phone use relates to face-to-face connection, wellbeing and sleep, and how time with close and distant contacts online related to stress during COVID-19.

name: Applied memory and cognition research
definition: Using what is known about memory, attention, and judgment to answer practical questions. Examples are how people hold on to information and how they weigh advice.
proof: In a graduate seminar, I turned theories of memory into a proposal for an applied study.

name: Socio-technical systems analysis
definition: Studying a technology together with the people, rules, and settings around it. Outcomes depend on all of them, not on the tool alone.
proof: In a graduate course, I traced how AI, cloud, and data systems depend on people and policy, through essays, a group project, and a final project.

name: Survey and questionnaire development
definition: Writing questions that people read the same way and can answer honestly, then testing and revising them before the survey goes out.
proof: I built the surveys for every study I have run and programmed them in Qualtrics. I wrote items for a published survey of why people play games.

name: Scale development and psychometrics
definition: Building a set of questions that measures one idea. The work has three parts: writing and checking the items, building the scale, and testing it. Testing covers how many ideas it captures (dimensionality), how consistent it is (reliability), and whether it measures what it claims (validity).
proof: I built the trust measures for my dissertation and a scale of how close people feel to their smartphones (in preparation, first author). I contributed to a published survey of gaming motivation and a VR symptom questionnaire.

name: Participant recruitment
definition: Finding and enrolling the right people for a study, in enough numbers, through online panels, campuses, clinics, or community groups.
proof: I recruit in person, through university pools, and on MTurk, CloudResearch and Prolific. I also handle recruitment administration for an NIH clinical trial.

name: Participant-centered communication
definition: Explaining a study, consent, and results in plain words. People can then decide for themselves whether to take part and know what happens to their information.
proof: I wrote the instructions and handled questions for general-public, student, online-panel and clinical-study participants.

name: Online-panel data quality
definition: Keeping careless and fake responses out of online studies. Attention checks and screening for bots and duplicates are set before data collection starts.
proof: I screen out inattentive and duplicate respondents. In a COVID-19 survey, 674 people consented and 569 completed it.

name: Behavioral intervention measurement
definition: Choosing and tracking the outcomes that show whether a program changed behavior, and by how much. The same measures are used before and after, and for every group.
proof: I designed dissertation Study 6, which tracked trust, adherence, and behavior for 15 days. It showed no reliable difference between the doctor and AI conditions, and I reported it that way.

name: Content and media coding
definition: Turning text, video, or images into data with a written coding scheme. Several coders apply it, and their agreement is checked.
proof: I coded video for prejudice in media, transcribed focus groups, and analyzed emotional speech in earlier lab roles.

name: Regression and multilevel modeling
definition: Estimating how an outcome moves with other variables. Multilevel models add random effects for data that are not independent, such as repeated answers from one person or students in the same classroom.
proof: I fit linear, logistic, ordinal, negative-binomial, and mixed-effects models. In one analysis I pooled eight experiments (1,778 people) into a single multilevel model.

name: Core statistical tests
definition: Choosing the standard test that fits the data, based on how many variables there are and what kind. T-tests compare averages, chi-square handles categories, correlation links two measures, and ANOVA compares three or more groups.
proof: I run t-tests, ANOVA (including repeated-measures designs), planned contrasts and chi-square tests, and I report effect sizes with them. I used them in my thesis, my dissertation, my graduate statistics courses, and a CSUN analysis of probation students' GPA.

name: Mediation and moderation
definition: Testing how an effect works and for whom it holds. A mediator is the middle step that carries the effect, and a moderator is a condition that makes it stronger or weaker. One model can test both.
proof: I tested who is affected and why. My dissertation used a multilevel mediated-moderation model, and my generative AI preprint used causal mediation.

name: Subgroup and group-difference analysis
definition: Comparing outcomes across groups of people and testing whether a relationship holds in each one. The aim is to show where results differ and for whom.
proof: At CSUN I compared how unit load related to GPA, retention and graduation for athletes, Pell recipients, and students served by disability services. At Georgetown I compared class size by student rank, faculty type, and demographic group.

name: Structural equation modeling
definition: Testing a whole set of relationships at once, including ideas that cannot be measured directly. The model is then checked for how well it fits the data.
proof: I built latent-variable path models for an award-winning data competition entry, replicated a published model in R for a graduate course, and ran Mplus models for my dissertation.

name: Power and sensitivity analysis
definition: Working out how many people a study needs to detect an effect of a given size, often with an 80% chance. After a study ends, the same math shows which effect sizes it could have detected.
proof: I plan sample sizes before each study and check what each one can detect. I taught a power-analysis workshop in 2023.

name: Robustness checks
definition: Re-running an analysis with other reasonable choices, such as different exclusions or models, to see whether the conclusion holds.
proof: In my generative AI research, I tested the main result across 69 alternative analyses, so the conclusion does not rest on one analysis choice.

name: Blind outcome rating
definition: Having judges score work without knowing which condition produced it. That keeps their expectations from shaping the scores.
proof: I designed blind ratings for my generative AI preprint. Judges who did not know the condition rated the work, and I compared quality with time spent.

name: Cross-study data integration
definition: Combining data from separate studies into one dataset. The measures and coding are matched first, so the studies can be analyzed together.
proof: I pooled eight experiments for a published analysis. Along the way I found and removed 173 placeholder rows.

name: Data cleaning and quality control
definition: Checking raw data for errors, duplicates, impossible values, and missing answers. Every change is documented so the analysis can be repeated.
proof: I prepared the data for a study of fans and their favorite characters, for the pooled analysis, and for more than 100,000 student records. At CSUN I profiled duplicate records, confirmed where they came from, removed the true duplicates, and reported the limits.

name: Data visualization and dashboards
definition: Showing data in charts and interactive pages so a reader can see patterns, compare groups, and check the numbers.
proof: I built Tableau dashboards that department chairs and administrators used each semester, and I made the figures for my generative AI preprint and this website.

name: Student-success and institutional analytics
definition: Using student and institutional records to answer questions about how courses, workloads, and programs relate to grades, retention, and graduation. The goal is evidence that administrators can use.
proof: At CSUN Institutional Research I analyzed how unit load and course format related to GPA, retention and graduation, including more than 630,000 course grades with controls for student background. At Georgetown I analyzed class size and teacher time.

name: Bayesian inference
definition: Weighing how strongly the data support one hypothesis over another, using a number called the Bayes factor. Unlike a p-value alone, it can show evidence for no effect as well as for an effect.
proof: I use Bayes factors and Bayesian t-tests to show how strongly the data support a null result. They appear in my generative AI preprint and on the Studies 1 and 2 pages of this site.

name: Latent profile analysis
definition: Finding hidden subgroups of people who share a pattern across several measures. The groups are not defined in advance, and the data reveal them.
proof: I completed a 2023 workshop on latent profile analysis, a method that sorts people into groups by their pattern of answers.

name: Classification and model evaluation
definition: Building a model that sorts cases into groups, then testing it on data the model has not seen. The test shows how often it is right and what its mistakes cost.
proof: I built and tested classifiers in an end-to-end Python project for a graduate course. My prediction work outside coursework is regression-based, such as a poster on predicting app use.

name: Economic and cost-benefit analysis
definition: Comparing what a program costs with the value of what it produces, in money or in outcomes gained.
proof: I applied cost-benefit and market-failure analysis to policy questions in two graduate economics courses.

name: R, Stata and SPSS
definition: Statistical software for cleaning data, running models, and producing results that others can repeat.
proof: R is my main language for modeling, figures and teaching. I used Stata across a graduate sequence in regression and program evaluation.

name: Cloud and API experiment engineering
definition: Connecting a survey tool to cloud services and AI model interfaces. The experiment can then randomize people, call a model, and record every response automatically.
proof: I host research tasks in the cloud and connect them to survey software. For one study, AWS linked Qualtrics to the ChatGPT API and stored each prompt and response.

name: Text analysis with dictionaries
definition: Counting words from fixed word lists, such as emotion or social words, to measure what a piece of writing is about. The counts are checked against human reading.
proof: I ran LIWC text analysis at a university lab in 2018 and 2019.

name: Web, design and automation tools
definition: Building web pages and graphics, and writing scripts that automate repeated work.
proof: I wrote Excel macros and Praat scripts in earlier lab work. I build web pages, slides, and posters, including mrleitao.com and this site.

name: Modern text analysis
definition: Using language models and similar tools to measure meaning, similarity, and topics in large amounts of text. The output is validated against careful human reading.
proof: In my generative AI preprint, I compared human and AI writing with similarity scores. I also took a 2023 text-analytics workshop and a graduate course on word-frequency methods (TF-IDF) and language processing.

name: Python
definition: A general-purpose programming language used for cleaning data, running analyses, and automating tasks.
proof: I used pandas, Jupyter, web scraping, and scikit-learn in a graduate data-science course. R is the language I use daily.

name: SQL
definition: The language for pulling and combining data stored in databases.
proof: I am building SQL skills through structured self-directed practice on DataLemur and Mode Analytics, and by translating my R code into SQL.

name: Geospatial analysis
definition: Analyzing data tied to places, such as mapping where outcomes occur and how they vary by location.
proof: I mapped open Los Angeles County data in ArcGIS for a 2018 data competition entry.

name: Human-AI trust and reliance research
definition: Studying when and why people accept, reject, or lean too heavily on advice from AI, compared with advice from a human expert.
proof: My six-study dissertation compares trust in doctors and medical AI. It measures reliance by how far people move their own answer toward the advice.

name: Human-AI collaboration experiments
definition: Testing how splitting a task between a person and an AI changes the quality of the work and how the person feels about it. Who drafts and who edits is one example.
proof: I am co-first author on a preprint with two experiments (1,299 people) on drafting with generative AI versus editing its output. Work quality was similar. How people experienced the work was not.

name: Obedience to computer authority
definition: Studying whether people follow a computer's instructions the way they follow an authority figure's.
proof: My master's thesis (305 participants) tested whether people obey computer instructors as readily as human ones. People obeyed both about equally, and I reported the null result.

name: Health and risk communication research
definition: Studying how health information and risk are explained, understood, and acted on, including what people do with test results.
proof: I study how people read genetic-risk information. On a virtual-patient project (200 participants), I collected, cleaned, and analyzed the data.

name: Research program management
definition: Keeping a group of related studies on schedule, on budget, and pointed at the same research goals.
proof: I managed six to seven projects at once at Georgetown with a student team, and I now support six NIH projects.

name: Study operations
definition: Running a study day to day: scheduling, collecting data, tracking progress, and fixing problems as they come up.
proof: I run studies from ethics approval through launch, monitoring and data handoff, for my own projects and for NIH collaborators.

name: Supervising and mentoring
definition: Directing other people's work, giving feedback, and helping them build skills. Research assistants are a common example.
proof: I have supervised research assistants since 2017, on teams of up to 15. I guided an honors thesis and served as a graduate mentor for a national psychology society.

name: Research governance
definition: Following the rules that protect research participants: ethics review, consent, and approved protocols. They rest on three principles, respect for persons, beneficence, and justice.
proof: I wrote and managed ethics-board protocols at two universities and support regulated clinical-study administration at NIH.

name: Clinical-study administration
definition: Handling the paperwork and compliance for a study with patients, including approved protocols, consent, enrollment records, and reporting. The work follows the ethics rules for human subjects research.
proof: I support participant recruitment for an NIH clinical trial that tests a drug.

name: Recruitment operations
definition: Managing the pipeline that brings participants into a study: outreach, screening, scheduling, and follow-up.
proof: I coordinated the Georgetown research participant pool and combined in-person, university and online recruitment.

name: Workflow and process improvement
definition: Finding where routine work is slow or error-prone and redesigning it to be faster and more consistent.
proof: As co-coordinator of the Georgetown participant pool, I helped redesign how it worked, and research yield rose 50% over the previous year. I also built reusable lab templates.

name: Grants and budgets
definition: Planning what a project will cost and tracking spending against the funding.
proof: I won three named grants and fellowships, and I wrote the budgets and timelines for my funded and independent research.

name: Grant-proposal writing
definition: Writing the case for funding: the question, the plan, the budget, and why the work matters.
proof: I wrote full proposals in graduate seminars, including a three-study program, and I presented grant literature at a university lab.

name: Policy analysis and memos
definition: Weighing evidence on a policy question and writing a short memo that gives decision makers a clear recommendation.
proof: I served on the task force whose recommendation on storing and showing gender identity and pronouns became policy. With another graduate student I built the evidence on how well the GRE predicted first-year grades and presented it to faculty and administrators. My program then made the GRE optional. In graduate work I wrote policy memos and testimony.

name: Consultative analysis
definition: Answering a client's question with data. That means framing the problem, choosing the method, and presenting findings the client can act on.
proof: With a self-managed team, I interviewed an organization and wrote a 20 to 30 page consulting report in a graduate course.

name: Curriculum and course design
definition: Planning what a course teaches, in what order, and how learning will be assessed.
proof: I designed and taught Psychology of Technology as instructor of record. It won Georgetown's 2023 Graduate Student Teaching Award.

name: Teaching across settings
definition: Teaching in classrooms, labs, workshops, and online, and adjusting to each group of learners.
proof: I have taught at Georgetown and Kaplan, assisted and tutored at CSUN, led recitations, and given guest lectures in people analytics and learning analytics.

name: Workshop design and facilitation
definition: Planning and leading a short, hands-on session so participants leave able to do something new.
proof: I taught workshops on power analysis, R and open science, then Introduction to R and Quarto at NIH.

name: Documentation and reusable resources
definition: Writing guides, templates, and code notes so other people can repeat the work without asking.
proof: I made public R, Quarto and power-analysis materials on OSF and lab templates that others can reuse.

name: Scientific writing
definition: Writing papers and reports that state the question, the method, and the results clearly and completely.
proof: I wrote all of my thesis and dissertation, and I contributed writing to several published papers.

name: Technical translation
definition: Explaining statistical or technical results to people outside the field without losing accuracy.
proof: I turn statistics into plain recommendations for papers, talks, dashboards, workshops and policy discussions.

name: Public science communication
definition: Sharing research with the general public in plain language, through talks, writing, or media.
proof: I taught students to write a magazine-style article from a research paper, and I explain my own work in plain words on this site.

name: Talks and speaking
definition: Presenting work to an audience, from conference talks to team briefings, and answering their questions.
proof: I chaired a 2024 conference session on AI, and gave invited talks at the University of Virginia and a film festival.

name: Building with LLM APIs
definition: Writing software that sends requests to a large language model and uses its answers inside a tool or study.
proof: I built the task for my generative AI preprint on the ChatGPT API. Each participant got a live AI response, and every exchange was logged.

name: AI-assisted analysis and coding
definition: Using an AI assistant to speed up writing code and analysis, with a person checking every output.
includes: Checking AI output against the data
proof: I used generative AI to run 69 alternative analyses of the main result in my generative AI research. I also use it to build code and figures, including this website, and I check its output against the data.

name: AI coding assistants
definition: Using an AI assistant to draft code, check it, and explain it, while keeping responsibility for what the code does.
proof: I am familiar with Claude, Claude Code and ChatGPT for coding and analysis. I use them for specific tasks, not as a daily tool, and I check what they write.

name: AI workflow automation
definition: Setting up repeatable steps, written rules, and small tools so an AI assistant does routine work reliably.
includes: Written rules and project files for an AI assistant
proof: I built a job-search workflow around an AI assistant, with written rules, a scoring scheme, and daily triage. I also build small tools of my own, such as a task-priority app.

name: Evaluating AI output
definition: Testing whether AI answers are accurate and useful, using blind ratings, comparison sets, and clear criteria.
proof: I designed blind ratings for my generative AI preprint. Judges who did not know the condition scored the work, and I compared quality, time, and how closely people's text matched the AI's.

name: Ownership
definition: Taking responsibility for a piece of work from start to finish, including its problems.
proof: I carried my thesis and six-study dissertation from the first question through design, recruitment, analysis and writing.

name: Project leadership
definition: Setting a project's direction, assigning the work, and keeping it moving to the finish.
proof: I built a student team, delegated work, and kept six to seven projects moving at once.

name: People leadership
definition: Guiding a team by setting expectations, giving feedback, and supporting each person's growth.
proof: I have supervised research assistants since 2017. My teams reached 14 to 15 people.

name: Prioritization
definition: Deciding which tasks come first when time and resources are limited.
proof: I handed off secondary projects to protect my dissertation deadlines and kept the wider research moving.

name: Mentorship and development
definition: Helping others grow their skills through advice, feedback, and chances to practice.
proof: I guided an undergraduate honors project from start to finish and supported a former student's conference project.

name: Team science
definition: A collaborative effort to address a scientific challenge. It draws on the strengths and expertise of people trained in different fields.
proof: I work with teams in psychology, medicine, genomics, policy, business and clinical research, and completed formal team-science training.

name: Stakeholder communication
definition: Keeping the people who depend on or fund the work informed, in the form and level of detail they need.
proof: I represented graduate students to faculty, answered participants, and explained results to learners, administrators and collaborators. When stakeholders disagree with the results, I respect their experience and show them the data.

name: Facilitation
definition: Guiding a group conversation so everyone contributes and the meeting ends in a decision.
proof: I ran workshops, guest lectures, a journal club and class discussions, and set the rules for respectful disagreement in my course.

name: Collaborative authorship
definition: Writing papers with co-authors: dividing the sections, merging edits, and agreeing on credit.
proof: I have worked as first, co-first, middle and contributing author across labs and spelled out each contribution.

name: Advocacy and representation
definition: Speaking up for a group or cause and bringing its needs into decisions.
proof: I served on the diversity committee and data-governance task force and brought student needs and evidence into policy discussions.

name: Audience awareness
definition: Fitting the message, the detail, and the wording to the person reading or listening.
proof: I design participant instructions, course assignments and technical materials for readers with different backgrounds.

name: Methodological judgment
definition: Choosing the right design and analysis for the question, and knowing what the data can and cannot show.
proof: I match the analysis to the question: count models for counts, multilevel models for nested data, scale methods for measures, causal designs for cause.

name: Honest reporting
definition: Reporting what the data show, including results that did not work, without overstating them.
proof: I reported null results as nulls in my thesis and in dissertation Study 6, disclosed changes to my plans, and stated the limits of each design.

name: Learning from null results
definition: Treating a finding of no effect as information: asking why, and using the answer to design the next study.
proof: After my thesis null result, I studied what it implies for authority in new situations. Each dissertation study refined the one before.

name: Ethical judgment
definition: Seeing the ethical side of a decision and choosing the course that respects people, limits harm, and treats them fairly.
proof: I weigh evidence against values, rights and fairness in policy work, and studied privacy, accountability and bias in data courses.

name: Ethical risk assessment
definition: Identifying how a study or tool could harm people, weighing that against its benefits, and putting safeguards in place first.
proof: My studies involved deception, participant discomfort, clinical samples, and genetic-risk data. I examined cases where trust in AI is too high or too low.

name: Systems thinking
definition: Seeing how the parts of a larger system affect one another, so a fix in one place does not break another.
proof: In the participant pool I connected participant experience, researcher needs, recruitment rules and course credit into one system.

name: Initiative and community building
definition: Starting useful work without being asked and bringing people together around it.
proof: I co-founded an open-science group and a journal club and started workshops that keep running.

name: Adaptability
definition: Changing the approach when plans, tools, or conditions change.
proof: I moved research, teaching and collaboration online during the pandemic and kept delivering.

name: Continuous learning
definition: Keeping skills current by picking up new methods and tools as the field moves.
proof: I trained in management, team science, latent profiles, text analytics and longitudinal methods, then used them where I could.
